content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Now building the before/after comparison page for the PR.

**Design plan** — utilitarian, subject is a schema diagram tool:
- **Color**: ink `#15191E`, paper `#FCFCFB`, muted `#6C7580`, rule `#DCE1E6`, accent blueprint-blue `#2E6E8E`, before-marker rust `#A8552E`
- **Type**: system sans for prose, `ui-monospace` for measurements and class names — the page is full of pixel values, so tabular figures throughout
- **Layout**: stacked before/after pairs at full width (the defect is only visible at size), each with a finding strip; a measurements table below

input.command:
gh pr create --repo lobu-ai/owletto --base main --head feat/schema-graph-legibility --title "feat(owletto): make the schema map legible and author from its panel" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What

The Memory schema map (`/$owner/memory`) was unreadable past a handful of types. Three separate defects, all visible in one screenshot: relationship labels collided into each other, long type names truncated to `Comp…`, and the unconnected-types column pushed the actual schema into a corner.

**Before / after screenshots + measurements:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/28ab10d9-2359-41e1-805d-c3b5f39d562e

## Legibility

- **Bundle by pair, not by relationship type.** Every relationship between the same two types now shares one path — 6 paths become 3 on the reference workspace. A bundled path shows a count pill.
- **Names leave the resting canvas.** They are disclosed on hover, on tap (edges are selectable and focusable), and through `aria-label`, so the disclosure is not mouse-only.
- **Boxes size themselves** from measured title and meta text, clamped 200–320px, with the name on its own line. It had shared a row with the counts and was the only flexible item on it, so identity was always what lost space to metadata.
- **`fitView` frames the connected subgraph**, so islands cannot push the schema off screen.

## Authoring moved into the panel

The relationship form was a modal that covered the very boxes you pick between — its two inputs are From and To. Editing a type navigated away to `/$owner/entity-types/$slug`, hiding the map being edited. Both now render beside the canvas.

`EntityTypePage` is reused verbatim rather than reimplemented narrow; it gains a `compact` prop for the heading. The routed page stays — the entity-type rail still links to it.

## Resizable divider

---
name: reference-owletto-vitest-projects-and-localstorage
description: owletto vitest splits node/jsdom by file extension, and jsdom 29 has NO localStorage — persistence tests need a Storage stub
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`packages/owletto/vitest.workspace.ts` routes by extension, not by content:
`src/**/*.test.ts` → the `node` project (no `window`), `src/**/*.test.tsx` → the
`jsdom` project. A `.test.ts` that touches `window` fails with
`ReferenceError: window is not defined`. Override per file with a
`// @vitest-environment jsdom` docblock — it works and does switch the
environment, even though the runner still labels the file `|node|`.

**jsdom 29 has no `localStorage` at all** — it delegates Web Storage to Node's
implementation, which stays inert unless the runner is started with
`--localstorage-file`. Verified in both projects: `typeof window.localStorage`
is `undefined` on a proper `http://localhost:3000` origin.

This matters because `src/lib/storage.ts` (`getStored`/`setStored`) wraps
everything in try/catch and returns `null` on failure. So a persistence test
does not fail loudly — it **passes vacuously** against a null read, or asserts
nothing at all. Install a Storage stub with `Object.defineProperty(window,
"localStorage", {...})` and restore it in `afterAll`.

**How to apply:** any test asserting on persisted UI state (panel widths, view
preferences, dismissed banners) must stub Storage first, or it is testing the
private-mode fallback rather than the feature. See
[[feedback-guards-must-assert-coverage]] and
[[feedback-mutation-test-new-tests]] — a mutation run is what exposes this,
since removing the persistence entirely still leaves the test green.

content.text:
Done. **PR: https://github.com/lobu-ai/owletto/pull/648** — one PR, 15 files, +1772/−482.

**Comparison page:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/28ab10d9-2359-41e1-805d-c3b5f39d562e

## On "why more PRs"

You were right about the split I proposed — I folded all four concerns into one branch. The concern is "make the Memory schema page usable," and legibility, panel authoring, the divider, and the redundant chip all serve it.

But there's one more PR I can't avoid, and it's structural, not a judgment call: **`packages/owletto` is its own repo** (`lobu-ai/owletto`), included as a submodule. So the code PR lands there, and the parent `lobu` repo then needs a separate PR that only moves the submodule pointer. Owletto merges first. That's two PRs for mechanical reasons, not scope reasons.

## The divider drags now

`role="separator"` between canvas and panel, doubling as the border. Verified against the prod backend:

| Gesture | Panel | Canvas |
|---|---|---|
| Rest | 288 | 799 |
| Drag left 150px | 438 | 649 |
| Reload | 438 | restored |
| Drag past window edge | 720 | 367 |
| Same, in a 1060px window | 387 | **320 exactly** |
| Double-click | 288 | override cleared |

A drag beats the mode default permanently — reverting to 440 when the editor opens would read as the handle being broken. Arrows nudge 16px, Home resets. Hand-rolled: no new dependency for `startWidth - dx` clamped.

## Two real bugs caught, one of them mine

`make review-fix` found that clamping against the flex **row** width overstates available space by the handle plus two gaps. I measured it live: row 1116 vs usable 1087, a 29px error that would have let the canvas drop below its promised floor. Now it measures `canvas.clientWidth + panel.clientWidth` — and the narrow-window test lands on exactly 320.

It also caught that in the **empty state** (zero types) my "Create entity type" button set a panel mode with no panel rendered — the same class of dead-click you found on mobile, in a branch I hadn't checked. Kept as a route there, since with no map to preserve the panel has no reason to exist.

I reviewed all five of its fixes against the source rather than taking the summary; the tap-to-reveal it added doesn't undo the legibility work — 2 count-pills at rest, names still off the canvas, now reachable by tap and screen reader instead of hover only.

## Verification

1128 tests pass, `tsc` clean, `make pre-pr` clean. I mutation-tested the new tests — flipped the drag direction, dropped the button guard, made the drag lose to the default, removed the canvas floor, unhid the handle on mobile. All five caught.

One correction worth flagging: my persistence tests were initially passing against nothing. jsdom 29 here has **no `localStorage` at all**, and `lib/storage.ts` swallows that into a null return — so the assertions were vacuous until I stubbed Storage. Saved to memory.

## Confidence

- **85 — resize, mobile, legibility.** Driven at real viewports against prod with DOM measurements; the clamp verified at the window size where it actually binds.
- **80 — the fixer's corrections.** Read the source and re-verified both live.
- **55 — save.** Unchanged and unproven. I never submitted a form; that writes to your real workspace and the edit target was Company with 2,035 records.

## Next actions

- Let me prove save with a throwaway type, then delete it — the last real gap, and I'd want your go-ahead since it writes to prod.
- Merge #648, then I'll open the parent-repo pointer PR (that worktree is behind `origin/main` and needs a pull first).
- Prod-verify after rollout, gated on the squash commit.
- Vite is still up on `localhost:5174` against the prod backend if you want to drag it yourself.

content.text:
Done — the `Memory` label drops to `text-sidebar-foreground/50` when the accordion is open, so it reads as the parent of the type rows rather than another one of them.

**One judgment call worth surfacing:** I made it recede *only when it isn't carrying the highlight*. Three states:

| State | Memory label |
|---|---|
| Collapsed | Full weight — no children to be confused with |
| Open, on `/memory` itself | Full weight, highlighted — being the current page outranks being a parent, and grey-on-accent reads as disabled |
| Open, browsing a type | **Greyed** — the confusing case |

That third row is the one you're describing: once you click into Person or Company, Memory loses its highlight and becomes pixel-identical to its own children. That's where it looked like an entity type.

Verified against prod at all three: greyed reads alpha `0.5` vs Company's full-strength accent; the other two stay at `0.8`.

Mutation-tested the three new tests — never recede, recede whenever open (ignoring the highlight), recede always (ignoring open). Each was caught.

**Two things worth noting:**

I hit the stale-browser-module trap again — my first live check showed the class missing even though vite was serving the edited source. Restarting vite fixed it; the code was always right. Third time this session that a stale dev-server cache has produced a false negative.

And my first DOM probe was wrong in a way that would have misled me: I checked `className.includes("bg-sidebar-accent")`, which also matches `hover:bg-sidebar-accent/60` — so every row looked highlighted. The existing tests in this file carry a comment warning about exactly that. Switched to `classList.contains`.

I left the type rows at the same indent as Memory. Re-indenting them would be the other way to carry hierarchy, but you asked for the grey and that's a bigger layout change than the ask.

This is on the same branch as PR #648 rather than a new one, since you'd rather not fan out PRs — but it isn't pushed yet, so say the word if you'd rather it stood alone.

## Confidence

**High (85)** — verified at all three states against prod with computed colors, plus mutation-tested tests. The full suite is still running in the background; I'll flag it if anything unrelated broke.

## Next actions

- Push the sidebar commit to #648 once the suite reports green, and update the comparison artifact with the sidebar before/after.
- The save path is still unproven — happy to test it with a throwaway type if you want.
- Merge #648, then the parent-repo submodule-pointer PR.

cd /Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/.claude/worktrees/schema-graph-legibility/packages/owletto && gh pr edit 648 --repo lobu-ai/owletto --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What

The Memory schema map (`/$owner/memory`) was unreadable past a handful of types. Three defects visible in one screenshot: relationship labels collided into each other, long type names truncated to `Comp…`, and the unconnected-types column pushed the actual schema into a corner.

**Before / after screenshots + measurements:** https://claude.ai/code/artifact/28ab10d9-2359-41e1-805d-c3b5f39d562e

## Legibility

- **Bundle by pair, not by relationship type.** Every relationship between the same two types shares one path — 6 paths become 3 on the reference workspace. A bundled path shows a count pill.
- **Names leave the resting canvas.** Disclosed on hover, on tap (edges are selectable and focusable), and through `aria-label`, so the disclosure is not mouse-only.
- **Boxes size themselves** from measured title and meta text, clamped 200–320px, with the name on its own line. It had shared a row with the counts and was the only flexible item on it, so identity always lost space to metadata.
- **`fitView` frames the connected subgraph**, so islands cannot push the schema off screen.

## Authoring moved into the panel

The relationship form was a modal covering the very boxes you pick between — its two inputs are From and To. Editing a type navigated away to `/$owner/entity-types/$slug`, hiding the map being edited. Both now render beside the canvas.

`EntityTypePage` is reused verbatim rather than reimplemented narrow; it gains a `compact` prop for the heading. The routed page stays — the entity-type rail still links to it.

## Resizable divider

The panel picks a width by mode (288 index / 440 editor); the divider drags to override that. Persisted, clamped so the canvas keeps a 320px floor, `Home`/double-click to reset. A ResizeObserver re-clamps on mount and on container resize, so a width saved on a wide display does not restore oversized on a narrow one. Hand-rolled — `react-resizable-panels` would bring a layout engine to a problem that is `startWidth - dx` clamped.

## Bugs fixed

**1. "Create entity type" was dead below `lg`.** The panel was `hidden lg:flex`, so the button set a mode nothing rendered.

- **Red:** at 390px, clicking it produced no editor; panel computed `display: none`.
- **Green:** panel `flex w-full`, name input 358px, canvas `offsetParent === null`, Cancel restores the canvas. Regression test: `keeps the divider off a narrow viewport, where there is no split`.

**2. The expanded Memory sidebar row read as one of its own children.** It shared the type rows' weight, size and indent; browsing a type moves the highlight off it, leaving it indistinguishable from the list below. Now recedes to `text-sidebar-foreground/50` while it has children on screen — but stays full weight when collapsed, and when the map itself is the open page.

**3. Duplicate form ids.** Both responsive presentations of the relationship form can be mounted with CSS choosing the visible one, so fixed ids bound each label to whichever copy mounted first. Now `useId`-scoped.

The empty state (zero types) still routes to the create page rather than the panel — with no map to keep visible the panel's reason does not apply, and no panel is rendered to receive the mode.

## Also

Drops the `Needs setup` filter chip from Connectors. The list already sorts needs-setup first and badges each card, so the chip restated what was on screen. Eight filters remain.

## Testing

- `bunx vitest run` — **1133 passed**, 128 files. `tsc --noEmit` clean. Parent `make pre-pr` clean.
- New tests mutation-tested: flipped the drag direction, dropped the primary-button guard, made the drag lose to the mode default, removed the canvas floor, unhid the handle below `lg`, and three variants of the sidebar rule. All caught.

### Save path exercised end-to-end against production

Driven through the real UI against `app.lobu.ai` on a throwaway type, then cleaned up:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Create type in the panel | Node appeared on the canvas live, no navigation |
| Rename it in the panel | Box updated in place; panel handed its width back |
| Add relationship (`Works At` → Company) | Edges 3 → 4, cluster 3 → 4 members |
| Remove the rule | Only the read-only catalog entry left |
| Delete the type | Back to 14 nodes / 3 edges |

**Caveat:** entity-type deletion is a *soft* delete by design ("can be restored by a database administrator"), so a tombstoned row for `zz-scratch-deleteme` remains in the workspace. Nothing else was written; `Company` and every existing type were never edited.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

**owletto PR #648 is merged** (`df33325e`). The parent pointer PR is **lobu-ai/lobu#2365**, with `make review` running now — that posts the required `pi-review` status, so I'll merge once it reports.

## The save path is proven

You asked for it, so I ran it end to end against production on a throwaway type — never touching Company:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Create type in the panel | Node appeared on the canvas live, no navigation |
| Rename it | Box updated in place; panel handed its width back |
| Add `Works At` → Company | Edges 3 → 4, cluster 3 → 4 members |
| Remove the rule | Only the read-only catalog entry left |
| Delete the type | Back to 14 nodes / 3 edges |

That was the last real gap. Confidence on save goes from 55 to **90**.

**One residue you should know about:** entity-type deletion is a *soft* delete by design — the UI says "can be restored by a database administrator". So a tombstoned `zz-scratch-deleteme` row remains in the workspace. The visible state is exactly as I found it, but I can't claim the write left zero trace.

## What review-fix caught this round

Two were real bugs in my code, not style:

**A restored width wasn't re-clamped.** I only clamped during a drag, so a 720px panel saved on a wide display would restore oversized on a laptop — and `aria-valuemax` advertised a ceiling the container couldn't honour. Now driven by a ResizeObserver on the split row.

**The relationship form used fixed element ids.** Both responsive presentations can be mounted at once with CSS choosing the visible one, so each label bound to whichever copy mounted first. Now `useId`-scoped — visible in the DOM as `_r_d_-relationship`.

It also deleted four payload fields as unused. I checked that structurally rather than taking its word: `fieldCount`/`entityCount` still compose `metaLabel`, and edge-level `isSymmetric` still suppresses the arrowhead — only the dead node-payload copies went.

It again asked me to split out the connector changes. I kept them, per your call.

## Two things I got wrong

I ran a broad `pkill -f vitest` and may have killed a test run belonging to another worktree — there are several dev servers from other sessions on this machine. Scoped to my own PIDs after that.

And a DOM probe using `className.includes("bg-sidebar-accent")` matched `hover:bg-sidebar-accent/60`, making every sidebar row look highlighted. The existing tests in that file carry a comment warning about exactly this. Switched to `classList.contains`.

## Final state

1133 tests, `tsc` clean, parent `make pre-pr` clean. 17 files, +1900/−540 across three commits.

## Next actions

- I'll merge #2365 as soon as `pi-review` reports.
- After rollout, prod-verify the map on `app.lobu.ai`, gated on the squash commit (not the branch head).
- Worth a follow-up: that rule-removal `x` button has no accessible name — pre-existing, and I left it alone.

fix(owletto): reveal relationship names when an edge is reached by keyboard

Bundling the schema map's edges took relationship names off the resting
canvas and put them behind hover, a tap, and `aria-label`. Edges are tabbable,
so a keyboard user could reach one -- and nothing happened. Screen readers had
the names all along; sighted keyboard users had no way to get them.

React Flow fires neither `onEdgeClick` nor its own selection for a keypress on
a focused edge: measured in-browser, Enter and Space on a focused edge leave
the element unselected and emit no click. So nothing downstream of click or
selection could have carried this.

Focus is the keyboard's hover, so reveal on arrival rather than on a keypress.
React Flow owns the edge's `<g>` and exposes no prop on it, but it stamps the
edge id as `data-id`, and focus events reach the wrapper this component
already renders -- so the id is read on the way up instead of reaching into
the library.

Verified with real keystrokes against production: tabbing across three edges
reveals each one's names in turn and restores the counts on the ones left
behind; tabbing out to a button clears them.

Also corrects a test that claimed to cover keyboard users while only calling
`onEdgeClick` -- the very handler a keypress never reaches -- and teaches the
React Flow stub to render edges and nodes with the focusable, `data-id`
carrying shape the real library emits, so a focus test has something true to
run against.

Follow-up to #648, from a blocker its parent-repo review caught.

## The gap

#648 bundled the schema map's edges and moved relationship names off the resting canvas, behind hover, a tap, and `aria-label`. Edges are tabbable — so a keyboard user could reach one and **nothing happened**. Screen readers had the names via `aria-label` the whole time; sighted keyboard users had no way to get them.

## Why the obvious fix doesn't work

The review suggested syncing from React Flow's selection. Measured in-browser on the merged build, that would not have worked:

```
focus an edge   -> tabindex="0", document.activeElement === the edge   OK
press Enter     -> chips stay ["3","2"]      no reveal
press Space     -> chips stay ["3","2"]      no reveal
edge classList  -> "selectable" but NOT "selected"
```

React Flow fires neither `onEdgeClick` nor its own selection for a keypress on a focused edge. Nothing downstream of click or selection could carry this.

## The fix

Focus is the keyboard's hover, so reveal on arrival rather than on a keypress. React Flow owns the edge's `<g>` and exposes no prop on it, but it stamps the edge id as `data-id`, and focus events reach the wrapper this component already renders — so the id is read on the way up rather than reaching into the library.

`onBlurCapture` clears unconditionally: `focusout` on the element being left always precedes `focusin` on the one being entered, which I measured rather than assumed (`focusin:A → focusout:A → focusin:B`).

## Verified with real keystrokes against production

| Action | Focused | Canvas |
|---|---|---|
| Focus edge 1 | `pair:$member\|company` | `["Claims Identity Has Authority Proposes Merge With", "2"]` |
| Tab | `pair:$member\|$member` | `["3", "Claims Identity Proposes Merge With"]` |
| Tab | `pair:person\|company` | `["3", "2", "Works At"]` |
| Tab | a button | `["3", "2"]` — cleared |

Exactly one edge revealed at a time, following focus, restored on leaving.

## Tests

**Also fixes a test that lied.** #648 carried `lets touch and keyboard users reveal relationship names from an edge`, which only called `onEdgeClick` — the handler a keypress never reaches. It asserted nothing about keyboard users and would have passed with the bug present. Renamed to what it actually covers, and a real keyboard test added that drives focus through the rendered element.

That required teaching the React Flow stub to render edges and nodes with the focusable, `data-id`-carrying shape the real library emits — otherwise there is nothing true to focus.

Mutation-tested: dropping `focusedEdgeId` from the reveal predicate, removing the focus wiring, and removing the blur wiring are each caught. 1136 tests pass, `tsc` clean.
EOF

content.text:
I merged #648 before running the parent-repo review, and that review caught a real accessibility blocker. Fixing it forward as **owletto#650**, waiting on CI.

## The blocker was real, and mine

Bundling the edges took relationship names off the resting canvas. Edges are tabbable, so a keyboard user could reach one and **nothing happened**. Screen readers had the names via `aria-label` all along; sighted keyboard users had no path to them.

I reproduced it before touching code:

```
focus edge   → activeElement === the edge, tabindex="0"   ✓
press Enter  → chips stay ["3","2"]                       ✗
press Space  → chips stay ["3","2"]                       ✗
```

**The reviewer's suggested fix would not have worked.** It proposed syncing from React Flow's `onSelectionChange` — but the edge's classList after Enter reads `selectable` and *not* `selected`. React Flow never selects it, so nothing downstream of selection could carry this. Verifying the claim before acting on it is what surfaced that.

The fix reveals on **focus** instead — focus is the keyboard's hover. React Flow owns the edge `<g>` and exposes no prop on it, but stamps `data-id`, and focus events reach the wrapper I already render.

Verified with real Tab keystrokes against prod: three edges, each revealing its own names in turn, counts restored behind, cleared on tabbing out to a button.

## Two things my own tests got wrong

**A test that lied.** #648 shipped `lets touch and keyboard users reveal relationship names from an edge` — which only called `onEdgeClick`, the handler a keypress never reaches. It would have passed with the bug present. That's how this escaped. Renamed to what it covers, and a real keyboard test added that drives focus through the rendered element. That meant teaching the React Flow stub to emit the focusable, `data-id`-carrying shape the real library does.

**Two guards I wrote were speculative, and my comments overstated them.** Mutation testing showed a blur-ordering guard and a scoping check that no test could kill. Rather than write tests to justify them, I checked the actual behavior: `focusout:A` fires *before* `focusin:B`, so the guard was unnecessary — I'd had the ordering backwards in a code comment. Deleted it, simplified to an unconditional clear, and rewrote the scoping comment to say what's true (it states intent; node ids can't collide with `pair:` edge ids) rather than claim a bug it doesn't prevent.

1136 tests, `tsc` clean, three of four mutations caught — the survivor is a genuine no-op equivalence, not a gap.

## State

- **owletto#648** — merged (`df33325e`)
- **owletto#650** — open, keyboard fix, waiting on CodeRabbit
- **lobu#2365** — parent pointer, open, still points at `df33325e`. I'm holding it; once #650 merges I'll repoint and re-run `make review`.

## Confidence

**High (85)** on the keyboard fix — reproduced the bug, verified the fix with real keystrokes, mutation-tested.

**Lower on my process here (60).** I merged the submodule before the parent review ran, which is what let a blocker land on `main`. The right order is parent review first, then merge owletto — worth correcting for next time.

## Next

- Merge #650 when CI reports, repoint #2365, re-run `make review`, merge.
- Then prod-verify after rollout, gated on the squash commit.

## Blocker 2 — false positive, not fixing

The claim was that the Mac resume loop can never fire because the gateway has no matching contract. But that contract is in **PR #2361**, unmerged — I grepped its diff and found exactly the `status: "resume"` / `completeWindow not called — resume allowed` handling it says is missing. This is the second time this session a reviewer's suggested fix was wrong on the facts (the earlier one proposed syncing React Flow selection that never happens). Verifying before acting is what caught both.

## Why this keeps happening

Submodule pointer bumps are transitive: my one-line PR carries five owletto merges from several sessions, so `make review` audits all of them and hands me other people's blockers. That's the mechanism, not bad luck.

1. owletto#652 merges (Swift fix) — awaiting CI
2. Repoint lobu#2365 at the new owletto main

- Panel sizes by mode (288 index / 440 editor); a drag overrides both
  directions permanently. Reverting to the mode default when the editor opens
  reads as the handle being broken.
- Resize is hand-rolled — `react-resizable-panels` is not a dep and would bring
  a layout engine to `startWidth - dx` clamped.
- Clamp against `canvas.clientWidth + panel.clientWidth`, NOT the flex row:
  the row overstates by the handle + gaps (29px measured) and lets the canvas
  fall under its 320px floor. Re-clamp on mount + ResizeObserver, not only
  mid-drag, or a width saved on a wide display restores oversized.

  reviews the PARENT diff. owletto reports **no required checks** — `pi-review`
  is a parent-repo gate only, so owletto PRs ship on CodeRabbit + `[code]smith`.

  owletto first let a real a11y blocker reach `main`.

`completeBehaviorRun` synthesized `status: "completed"` for **any** 2xx body that failed to decode:

```swift
if let report = try? decoder.decode(BehaviorExitReport.self, from: data) {
    return report
```

- the current contract decodes as-is, resume and completion alike

The third blocker was real and I've fixed it in **owletto#653**, awaiting CI.

## The bug

`completeBehaviorRun` synthesized `status: "completed"` for *any* 2xx body that failed to decode. That call decides durable delivery state, so it breaks the fail-closed rule in `AGENTS.md` directly — a truncated payload, a 200 error envelope, or a proxy's HTML page all read as "the run finished," suppressing the resume the server was asking for.

Fixed to read the body without inventing an outcome: current contract decodes as-is; the one real legacy shape (2xx, minimal object, no `status`) is recognised explicitly and still rejected if it carries an `error` or `ok: false`; anything else throws. Throwing isn't a new failure mode — the dispatcher already catches and calls `completeWithError`, which is exactly the reconcilable failure the invariant wants.

Red→green: **7 failures** before, 0 after. Legacy `{"ok":true}` and `{}` pass in both, so older gateways are unaffected.

## I broke a hard invariant and repaired it

Mid-task the shell cwd reset to `~/Code/lobu` and my `cd packages/owletto` landed in the **main checkout** instead of the worktree. I ran `git checkout main`, `git reset --hard origin/main`, and created a branch there — a direct violation of "never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly."

No files were edited or committed there (my `Edit`/`Write` calls used absolute worktree paths), and nothing was pushed from it. I read the submodule reflog to find the exact prior state and restored it: branch `main` at `f61da939`, stray branch deleted, working tree clean. The dirty submodule pointer that remains was already there before I touched it — the parent expects `49a9909d` and it was sitting on `f61da939`.

The trap is that `cd` inside a compound command doesn't persist the way I assumed across tool calls. I'm using absolute paths and checking `pwd` from here.

## Blocker count so far

Three found by review, all in Mac Swift code from #647 — none in my schema-map work. Two real and fixed (#652, #653), one a false positive I'm not fixing (the resume loop's server contract is in #2361).

Each review round surfaces the next one because a pointer bump is transitive: my one-line PR audits five other merges.

## Remaining

1. Merge #653 when CI settles
2. Repoint #2365, re-run `make review`
3. Merge #2365 if clean
4. Flag #2361's rebase need
5. Prod-verify after rollout

If round four turns up a fourth Mac blocker, I'd suggest we stop fixing other people's code through my pointer PR and instead land the pointer at `23e49d72` — which contains all my work plus #652 — and let the Mac issues land on their own PR. Say the word if you'd rather do that now.

Found by the `pi-review` on lobu#2365.

## The bug

`LocalAgentDetector.searchPrefixes()` searches `$PATH` plus `~/.bun/bin`, `~/.local/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin`. Its own comment states why:

> Mirrors `LocalLobuRunner.preferredPath` / `locateLobuCLI` so detection and execution don't disagree.

They disagreed. `ClaudeCodeExecutor.locateOnPath` walked **`$PATH` alone**, and a LaunchAgent starts with a stripped `$PATH` — so a binary installed under `~/.bun/bin` or `/opt/homebrew/bin` was detected, advertised in the UI, possibly auto-selected, and then failed **every Behavior run** with `binary not found`.

**Wider than reported.** The review flagged `agy`, which at least had a hand-rolled `~/.local/bin` fallback covering one of the five dirs. `claude` had no fallback at all — it was the more exposed of the two.

## The fix

Route both through the detector's own list instead of adding a fourth copy. There were already three: the detector's, the child-process `PATH` the dispatcher injects, and `locateOnPath`'s. Now one list, so they cannot drift apart again. The redundant `~/.local/bin` special case in `AgyExecutor.resolveBinary` is deleted rather than left beside it.

`locateOnPath` takes the prefix list as a defaulted parameter so the walk is testable without touching real install dirs.

## Red / green

```
       apps/mac/Owletto/LocalAgentDetector.swift \
       apps/mac/Owletto/LobuClient.swift \
       apps/mac/Owletto/DeviceConnectorManifests.swift \
       apps/mac/Tests/BinaryResolutionTests.swift -o /tmp/t && /tmp/t

```


The test also pins that the shared list still carries every fallback dir, that `$PATH` keeps priority over them (so a user-installed shadow still wins over Homebrew), and that a same-named **non-executable** decoy never satisfies a lookup.

**Stated coverage limit:** the default argument binds `searchPrefixes()` at the call site and isn't observable from the test. It pins that the list carries the fallbacks and that the lookup walks what it's handed; the one-line binding between them is left to review.

---
name: project_make_review_verdict_reality
description: make review pi bug_free score ceilings ~82-88 for clean medium-risk changes; parallel reviews exhaust shared Codex quota + shm
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 93e0701a-244f-4186-ae24-16474025be81
  modified: 2026-07-29T08:10:00.020Z
---

`make review` (the pi verdict, gpt-5.5:high ×3) realities learned shipping the 5-PR audit-fix wave (#1066-#1070, 2026-05-26):

- **bug_free score ceilings ~82-88 for correct, behavior-changing PRs** even at **0 bugs / 0 blockers / no suggested fixes**. The gap to 90 is driven by `behavior_change_risk: medium`, not defects. The ×3 verdict has real run-to-run **variance** (one clean PR swung 88→82→88 with no code change). **Don't chase a strict >90 bar for medium-risk fixes** — treat `0 bugs / 0 blockers + green deterministic suites + a real E2E reproducer` as the merge bar. Chasing >90 by re-rolling is a variance lottery and wasted effort.
- **Running many `make review` in parallel exhausts the shared Codex GPT-5.5 quota** → HTTP 429 `usage_limit_reached`, credits balance 0, **primary window resets in ~4-5h** (300-min window). ~5 concurrent review sessions burned it for the rest of the day. **Serialize reviews** (one at a time), or you block every PR's verdict for hours. Check reset via the `X-Codex-Primary-Reset-At` epoch in the 429 body.
- Parallel reviews also **exhaust macOS SHMMNI=32** via embedded-PG (each review spins one up; orphans linger). Symptom: integration step `ECONNREFUSED`. Fix: `ipcrm` nattch=0 segments (see [[reference_local_server_integration_tests]]); the review log paths in `scripts/review.sh` are shared `/tmp/lobu-review-*.log` so concurrent runs in sibling worktrees corrupt each other's logs.
- **Each `make review` leaks its embedded-PG data dir into `$TMPDIR` (`lobu-test-pg-*`, tens of MB) and never cleans it.** Over a multi-PR/multi-worktree session they pile up — I hit **213 dirs = 69GB**, filling the data volume to 100% (`df /` is misleading — it shows the sealed system root; check `df $TMPDIR` / `/System/Volumes/Data`). Symptom: review fails with `pi did not produce a valid JSON verdict` (ENOSPC, NOT quota). Cleanup: `find "$TMPDIR" -maxdepth 1 -name 'lobu-test-pg-*' -type d -print0 | xargs -0 rm -rf` (zsh aborts a bare `rm $TMP/glob*` if any sibling glob has no match — use `find`, not glob). Clean after each central review run.
- **Dispatched fix-agents exit before their backgrounded `make review` finishes** (they arm a Monitor and end the turn). Capture verdicts centrally (poll the PR comment make review posts) rather than trusting the agent to wait; tell them to run review in the FOREGROUND.

Confirmed real leak fixed in #1070: the [[reference_pi_createagentsession_tools_names_only]] gotcha lets the agent's general bash inherit `WORKER_TOKEN`/`DISPATCHER_URL` (only just-bash + exec-jobs stripped them); fix = post-construction tool-swap in agent-worker `session-builder.ts`.

**`make review` (local) ≠ GitHub CI — a green local review does NOT mean CI is green.** Burned hard merging the 5-PR wave (#1066-#1070, 2026-05-26): all passed local `make review` but several were red in CI. Gaps:
- `make review` runs **vitest**, which **EXCLUDES the bun:test gateway suite** (`packages/server/src/gateway/**/__tests__`, run by CI's `integration` job). So gateway tests can pass locally (host has network) and hang/fail in CI. A new gateway test that drove the REAL Chat SDK telegram adapter (`chat.initialize()`) leaked a hung socket in CI's network sandbox → 30s timeout → poisoned the shared bun:test process → ~114 cascade. An 8-way concurrent DB test exhausted CI's constrained Postgres pool → every later test's setup blocked to its hook timeout (the 30s "hangs" were collateral; the 5s per-test timeout doesn't cover a setup-hook hang). Fixes: don't instantiate real networked adapters in tests (stub the webhook handler); cap test concurrency (8→2 still proves row-lock convergence).
- CI jobs `make review` never runs at all: `check-drift` (owletto submodule pin must be an ancestor of owletto/main — a stale/rebased branch can drift to an off-main pin → fix by aligning the gitlink to origin/main's pin), `format-lint` (`biome format --check` on the whole repo — pre-commit `biome check --write` only touches staged files, so unrelated unformatted files merged in via base still fail), `Security tests (bun:test)`, `sdk-e2e`, `connector-parity-smoke`, CodeQL.
- ALWAYS `gh pr checks`/`statusCheckRollup` before merging; never trust local review alone. Distinguish real failures from transient infra: GitHub action-download failures ("could not be found at the URI...Failed to download archive after 1 attempts" for setup-bun/ssh-agent) and Docker "502 Bad Gateway" are flakes → `gh run rerun <id> --failed`. Verify a failing run is on the CURRENT head (`gh run view <id> --json headSha`), not stale.
- Merging to `main` auto-deploys to prod (Flux). `--squash --admin` bypasses the REVIEW_REQUIRED branch-protection gate. Merge clean PRs first, riskiest last.

**`pi-review` can post `failure` on a verdict with 0 bugs and 0 blockers** (2026-07-28, PR #2241): description read `bug_free 86, simplicity 88, slop 0, bugs 0, 0 blockers; tests inadequate, high risk needs human approval`. It is a **policy gate**, not only a defect gate — `tests_adequate:false` + `behavior_change_risk:"high"` fails the required check by design. So "0 blockers" is NOT sufficient to merge, and `--admin`-ing past a *reported failure* is exactly what AGENTS.md forbids. The fix is to make the tests adequate: extracting workflow-embedded shell into a checked-in script with a table-driven suite flipped it. **`scripts/__tests__/*` are named EXPLICITLY in `ci.yml`, never globbed** — a new file there does not run until you add its own step, so a suite added to satisfy this gate can silently never execute.

**Review rounds are not monotonic** (same PR, 2026-07-28 #2235): five consecutive rounds each surfaced a genuine blocker (installed-worker resolver path → dangling `@lobu/core` type import → gitignored dist read in the lint job → stale top-level `types` → publish-time script stripping), verdict 35 → 32 → 93. Round N being clean-ish says nothing about N+1. Rounds 5-6 were the same root cause in opposite directions: first fix stripped ALL non-lifecycle scripts (over-broad — `@lobu/connector-worker` ships `dist/` so its `start` genuinely runs), correct answer was deriving runnability from `files`. Reaching 0 blockers required fixing the CLASS, not the instance.

`bug_free 77, simplicity 76, slop 5, bugs 0, 0 blockers`. **Zero defects.** All eight other required checks pass (integration, typecheck, unit, frontend, format-lint, migrations, check-drift, base-branch-guard).

`main` has `enforce_admins: true`, so `--admin` can't bypass it — and forcing past a *reported failure* is what `AGENTS.md` forbids anyway. I also confirmed from `scripts/review.sh` that `behavior_change_risk: high` does **not** gate (that was removed in #2332), so risk isn't the problem.

The reviewer's note: *"durable resume/retry orchestration lacks direct coverage; Swift tests exercise only helpers."* It wants dispatcher-level tests with a fake executor and stubbed `URLSession` covering resume→second spawn, transient delivery failure replaying the same `finalize_attempt`, and non-retriable delivery never sending a contradictory report.

That's the **Mac resume feature's own coverage gap** — #647's code, whose server contract lives in #2361. Points 2 and 3 turn on `finalize_attempt` semantics defined in that unmerged PR. I'd be inventing the contract I'm testing against, which is how you get tests that pass and prove nothing — exactly the failure mode I already hit once today with the keyboard test that called `onEdgeClick` and claimed to cover keyboards.

So I've stopped, as I said I would. Four Mac fixes deep is already further than my one-line pointer bump should have taken me.

1. **Let #2361 carry it.** It owns the Swift feature *and* already bumps the pointer. Its author has the contract; my schema-map work rides along in their pointer bump. Cleanest, costs nothing extra.
2. **I write the dispatcher tests anyway**, guessing at `finalize_attempt` semantics from #2361's diff. Gets #2365 merged independently, but the tests would be built on my reading of someone else's unmerged design.
3. **Raise `PI_REVIEW_MIN_BUG_FREE` scope** — not recommended; the gate is doing its job here.

I'd take option 1.

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. <!-- Per-repo agent rules loaded into every Claude Code session in this repo. Inlines AGENTS.md (shared project rules) first, then layers local-only notes below. User memory entries live under ~/.claude/projects/.../memory/. Don't add anything here unless it's only relevant to Claude agent specific. @AGENTS.md

content.content:
## Repo map
- Bun workspace under `packages/*`; TS source is in `src`, tests in `__tests__`.
- Main packages: `core` shared types/utils, `plugin-api` native plugin contracts, `plugin-host` deterministic plugin composition, `server` gateway + embedded runtime, `agent-worker` Lobu agent execution, `connectors` built-in connectors, `owletto` frontend submodule.
- Before editing a package, read its nearest `AGENTS.md` if present.
- `docs/GOTCHAS.md` collects the mechanical traps (build, SQL, testing, submodule, browser) that have each cost a debugging session. Skim the section for the surface you are touching before you start, and grep it when something looks inexplicable.

## Hard invariants
- **Never write to `~/Code/lobu` directly — work in a worktree.** Run `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` first, and never `git switch` in the main checkout.
- One branch = one concern (not one file). Tangential task → commit/push/open current work, then branch fresh from `main`. Split only for genuinely independent concerns or an unreviewable diff.
- **Multi-replica correctness is mandatory.** Never put shared required state in an in-memory Map/singleton another replica must read or mutate. If a feature relies on cross-pod visibility, use Postgres-mediated state/signal.
- **`events` is append-only.** Never `DELETE FROM events`; tombstone/supersede instead.
- **Never bulk-delete prod `organization` rows**, including zero-activity ones — empty-looking orgs are frequently real human signups. Surface them one at a time for confirmation.
- **Workers never receive real credentials.** They may receive only placeholders/proxied access. The only exceptions are device-pinned connectors and short-lived provider-derived credential leases (see `packages/server/AGENTS.md`); a durable stored credential is never one of them.
- Default to static `import`. New dynamic imports require measured cost justification here or in the package AGENTS plus a rationale comment at the call site. Tests may dynamically import after mocks.
  - Node-version gate exceptions: `packages/cli/bin/lobu.js` defers the existing CLI graph without duplicating it, and `packages/server/src/server-entry.ts` adds an 842-byte gate in front of the 4.34 MB server graph (measured 2026-07-24). Both call sites must stay dependency-free until their checks pass.
- Bug fixes require red→fix→green evidence, with both outputs pasted into the PR body. If you cannot reproduce, stop and report the dead end — do not ship a speculative fix.
- Never report done off a green typecheck. Boot it, exercise every branch you touched, clean up test data. If "compiles" is all you ran, say so explicitly.
- Gates are non-negotiable (sequence in "Ship a change" below). `make pre-pr` builds first — that build step is what protects against a stale-dist false green. `make review` is an LLM verdict only: it does NOT run typecheck/knip/tests and is not proof CI will pass.
- The agent-facing product name is **Behavior**; `watcher` is internal engine/DB vocabulary. It must not appear in MCP tool schemas/names/descriptions, ClientSDK discovery metadata, or the connector-sdk public reaction contract — `make pre-pr` fails on it. Internal identifiers (`actingWatcherId`, table/column names, comments) are fine.
- `make review-fix` is the unposted fixer pass and runs BEFORE the first `make review`; verify its diff and commit it. Never iterate `make review` as a find-fix loop — each posted round costs a review + CI cycle.
- Fix the class, not the instance: on the first hit, grep every other instance and fix in one pass — a diff-scoped reviewer only ever finds the next one. Same root cause twice = stop reviewing, grep-enumerate. A class-wide fix is in scope for the branch that found it and does not count as scope creep.
- **Fail closed on durable dispatch/delivery state.** When a durable coordination or delivery operation fails, its caller must not reinterpret the error as proceed/deliver/skip. Propagate a retry, defer, or terminal-failure outcome with a visible log; if the operation may already have succeeded, reconcile idempotently before retrying. Treat lock timeouts, pool errors, and ambiguous or expired rows as failures, not as "nothing changed."
- **Coordination design brake.** A change that needs a second lock, a second retry/deferral budget, or a prose termination argument to explain why it halts is patching a misplaced check — stop and re-derive where the decision belongs before adding mechanism. Find the chokepoint that already serializes the action (e.g. worker dispatch is serialized by `job-router` on the worker-SSE-owner pod) and put the check there; prefer deleting the state transition over coordinating it, and reuse queue-native retry over hand-rolled hold/requeue.
- **Stage by explicit path; never commit the whole tree of a worktree that hosted other work.** A commit is a snapshot — stale file copies silently revert already-merged PRs. After commit/rebase, `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` must equal the task's intended file list; extra files = stop. Verify a "reverts merged work" review finding by diff direction against `origin/main`, never dismiss it as merge-base noise.

## Ship a change
1. `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` → work in `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/`.
2. Reproduce the bug (red) before fixing it. Fix, then prove green.
3. Test: `make test-unit` (no DB) / `make test-integration` (needs `DATABASE_URL` with pgvector). One file: `bun test <path>`, or `cd packages/server && bunx vitest run <path>` for vitest suites.
4. `make pre-pr` — build, typecheck, knip, lint, exposed-surface naming.
5. `make review-fix` on the settled diff and verify what it changed — it edits the working tree, so re-read the files before trusting them.
6. Stage by explicit path (`git add -- <paths>`, never `-A`), commit, then confirm `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` is exactly your intended file list. Extra files = stop.
7. `git push -u origin <branch>` → `gh pr create` (fill `.github/pull_request_template.md`; conventional-commit title, e.g. `fix(server): …`).
8. `make review` **once** on the settled HEAD. It posts the `pi-review` status, which is a REQUIRED check.
9. Merge squash once CI is green: `gh pr merge <n> --squash --admin`. Never `--admin` past a check that has not reported.
10. Prod-visible surface? Verify it live after rollout. Set a self-rescheduling `ScheduleWakeup` (~1500s) carrying the rollout gate: poll the deployed SHA, then `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$MERGE_SHA" "$DEPLOYED_SHA"` with `MERGE_SHA=$(gh pr view <n> --json mergeCommit --jq .mergeCommit.oid)`. Two ways this gate silently never opens — **gate on the squash commit, not your branch head** (a squash merge writes a new commit with no ancestry link to the branch, so the branch head exits 1 forever: PR #2280 has identical trees and still fails), and **keep that argument order** (merge commit first; reversed, it accepts a stale deploy). Run the live check when it lands, and write the result back to memory.

## Agent workflow
- Do only what was asked. Delete ephemeral files you create. Do not create `*.md` unless asked.
- Prefer `bun`; do not use npm/yarn/pnpm for repo work.
- Fix unused params by deleting them, not `_`-prefixing.
- Never `git stash`; use WIP commits and squash later.
- Never resolve merge conflicts in the GitHub web UI (it has silently dropped 1000+ lines of feature work). Rebase locally against `origin/main`, then diff against the last real feature commit before squashing — except on submodule-pointer branches, where you must `git merge` (see `docs/GOTCHAS.md`, "Submodule & cross-repo").
- Run mandated gates automatically; never ask permission to run one.
- Show the diff, not a summary. Before claiming done — on your own work or a dispatched agent's — surface `git status` plus `git diff --stat <base>...HEAD`. An agent's self-report is a claim; the diff is the evidence.
- UI PRs owe before/after screenshots, and `gh` cannot upload images inline. Capture before shots from the unmodified branch and after shots from the same booted app (auth recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`), base64-embed the PNGs into one self-contained HTML comparison page, publish it as a claude.ai artifact, and link it from the PR.
- Any subagent with write access (Edit/Write/Bash) runs in its own worktree; only grep/read agents share the parent. Two writing agents must NEVER share a worktree — they overwrite each other's uncommitted work.
- Dispatch code-writing agents through `make task-setup NAME=<slug>` and brief them with the absolute `.claude/worktrees/<slug>/` path. Only task-setup does the submodule branch pinning, post-init `bun install`, `.env` copy, and port allocation.
- Do repetitive multi-file edits (renames, signature changes, import rewrites) inline or with one script. Reserve subagents for read-only breadth or genuinely isolated parallel work.
- Before adding an env var, grep for the one the codebase already reads. Do not rename existing vars to a "cleaner" convention unasked.
- Deleting code needs structural evidence (dangling import, completed migration, superseded impl). Low prod usage is not a delete signal; trace the workflow, not just the import graph — docs and help text are load-bearing too.
- **Absence is never proven by a grep on a working tree.** To prove code does *not* exist, run `git fetch -q origin && git grep <pattern> origin/main` — the fetch is load-bearing, `origin/main` itself goes stale. Applies to every existence check, including the deletion-evidence rule above.
- Slack link pasted (`slack.com/archives/…?thread_ts=`) → run `scripts/slack-thread-viewer.js "<link>"` first.
- To drive the user's real logged-in browser, use the paired Owletto extension — recipe in `docs/BROWSER_TESTING.md`. Do **not** assume CDP/browser-auth is required.
- Unsure in planning → ask before making conflicting or irreversible choices. Mid-execution, block on a question only for irreversible/destructive actions or decisions that are genuinely the user's; for reversible choices with a clear recommended option, take it and flag the choice in your summary.

## Session efficiency
- Never poll in the foreground (`sleep`/`until`/`while` wait loops, repeated `tail`). Run long waits (dev-server boot, CI, deploys) in the background and act on the completion notification.
- Prefer DOM reads (`get_page_text`, `read_page`, `javascript_tool`) over screenshots; screenshot only when visual layout itself is under test. Screenshots are the #1 context-bloat source.
- Read a file before editing it, and re-read it after any external change (a fixer pass, another agent, a rebase). Blind edits fail and cost a retry round-trip.
- Read PR status compactly: `gh pr view <n> --json number,title,isDraft,mergeStateStatus,reviewDecision` plus `gh pr checks <n> --required`. Never `--json statusCheckRollup` — measured on PR 2280 it is 7520 bytes against 861, 8.7x larger and less legible.
- Batch narrow fixes into one commit, verified once at the end of the batch — not per fix. It never justifies skipping a reproducer or a correctness-critical test. For a one-line or config-only change, take one CI snapshot and move on.
